(j) processing is necessary for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes in accordance with Art. 89(1) based on Union or Member State law which is proportionate to the aim pursued, respects the essence of the right to data protection and provides for suitable and specific measures to safeguard the fundamental rights and the interests of the data subject. Art. 9(3): data referred to in paragraph 1 may be processed for the purposes of paragraph 2(h) when processed by or under the responsibility of a professional subject to the obligation of professional secrecy under Union or Member State law. Art. 9(4): Member States may maintain or introduce further conditions, including limitations, with regard to the processing of genetic data, biometric data or data concerning health.
237.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

238.text: Article 12: The controller must take appropriate measures to provide information and communications relating to processing to the data subject in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language. The controller must facilitate the exercise of data subject rights and provide information on action taken on a request without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two further months where necessary taking into account the complexity and number of requests. Information is provided free of charge unless requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive. GDPR Art. 15 - Right of access by the data subject: The data subject has the right to obtain confirmation as to whether personal data concerning them are being processed and, where that is the case, access to the data and information on the purposes, categories of data, recipients, the retention period, the existence of rights to rectification, erasure, restriction and objection, the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, the source of the data, and the existence of automated decision-making. The controller must provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing; for further copies it may charge a reasonable fee based on administrative costs. Where the request is made electronically, the information is provided in a commonly used electronic form.
238.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

239.text: Article 17 - Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten'): The data subject has the right to obtain erasure of personal data without undue delay where the data are no longer necessary for the purposes collected, consent is withdrawn and there is no other legal ground, the data subject objects and there are no overriding legitimate grounds, the data have been unlawfully processed, erasure is required to comply with a legal obligation, or the data were collected in relation to information society services offered to a child. Art. 17(3) exceptions: the right does not apply to the extent processing is necessary for exercising freedom of expression and information; for compliance with a legal obligation or a task in the public interest; for reasons of public interest in the area of public health in accordance with Art. 9(2)(h) and (i) and Art. 9(3); for archiving, scientific or historical research or statistical purposes where erasure would render impossible or seriously impair the objectives; or for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims. GDPR Art. 20 - Right to data portability: The data subject has the right to receive the personal data concerning them which they have provided to a controller in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance, where processing is based on consent or a contract and is carried out by automated means. Where technically feasible, the data subject may have the data transmitted directly from one controller to another.
239.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

240.text: Article 22 - Automated individual decision-making, including profiling: (1) The data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them. (2) Paragraph 1 does not apply if the decision is necessary for entering into or performing a contract, is authorised by Union or Member State law which lays down suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights, freedoms and legitimate interests, or is based on the data subject's explicit consent. (3) In the cases of contract and explicit consent, the controller must implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights, including at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express their point of view and to contest the decision. (4) Decisions referred to in paragraph 2 must not be based on special categories of personal data referred to in Art. 9(1), including data concerning health, unless Art. 9(2)(a) or (g) applies and suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights are in place. This is relevant to AI-based clinical decision support and insurance underwriting.
240.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

241.text: Article 25 - Data protection by design and by default: (1) Taking into account the state of the art, the cost of implementation and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risks to individuals, the controller must, both at the time of determining the means for processing and at the time of the processing itself, implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, designed to implement data-protection principles, such as data minimisation, in an effective manner and to integrate the necessary safeguards into the processing. (2) The controller must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed. That obligation applies to the amount of personal data collected, the extent of their processing, the period of their storage and their accessibility. In particular, such measures must ensure that by default personal data are not made accessible without the individual's intervention to an indefinite number of natural persons. (3) An approved certification mechanism may be used as an element to demonstrate compliance.
241.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

242.text: Article 28 - Processor: The controller may use only processors providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures. Processing by a processor must be governed by a contract or other legal act that is binding on the processor and sets out the subject-matter, duration, nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller. The contract must stipulate that the processor: processes personal data only on documented instructions from the controller; ensures persons authorised to process are committed to confidentiality; takes all measures required under Art. 32; respects conditions for engaging another processor (sub-processor) and remains fully liable to the controller for the sub-processor; assists the controller with data subject requests and with Articles 32 to 36; deletes or returns all personal data at the end of the services; and makes available all information necessary to demonstrate compliance and allows audits. This is the GDPR counterpart of the HIPAA business associate agreement.
242.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

243.text: Article 33 - Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority: In the case of a personal data breach, the controller must without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the competent supervisory authority, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Where notification is not made within 72 hours, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay. The processor must notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a breach. The notification must describe the nature of the breach including categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and records, the contact point of the data protection officer, the likely consequences and the measures taken or proposed. The controller must document all breaches. GDPR Art. 34 - Communication to the data subject: When the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller must communicate the breach to the data subject without undue delay in clear and plain language. Communication is not required if the data were rendered unintelligible by measures such as encryption, if subsequent measures ensure the high risk is no longer likely to materialise, or if it would involve disproportionate effort, in which case a public communication is used instead.
243.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

244.text: Article 35 - Data protection impact assessment: Where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller must, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data. A DPIA is required in particular for: a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, on which decisions are based that produce legal or similarly significant effects; processing on a large scale of special categories of data referred to in Art. 9(1), which includes data concerning health, or of data relating to criminal convictions; and systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale. The assessment must contain at least a systematic description of the processing and its purposes, an assessment of necessity and proportionality, an assessment of the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, and the measures envisaged to address the risks, including safeguards and security measures. The controller must seek the advice of the data protection officer and, where the DPIA indicates a high residual risk, consult the supervisory authority before processing (Art. 36).
244.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

245.text: Chapter V - Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations (Articles 44 to 49): Any transfer may take place only if the conditions of Ch. V are complied with by the controller and processor, so that the level of protection guaranteed by the Regulation is not undermined. Art. 45 - adequacy decisions: a transfer may take place where the European Commission has decided that the third country, territory or sector ensures an adequate level of protection. No specific authorisation is needed. Art. 46 - appropriate safeguards: in the absence of an adequacy decision, a transfer may take place subject to enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies through standard contractual clauses adopted by the Commission, binding corporate rules (Art. 47), approved codes of conduct or certification mechanisms, and other listed instruments. Following the Schrems II judgment, exporters must assess whether the third country's laws undermine the safeguards and add supplementary measures where needed. Art. 49 - derogations for specific situations: explicit consent after being informed of the risks; necessity for a contract; important reasons of public interest; legal claims; vital interests of the data subject who is physically or legally incapable of giving consent; and public registers. These derogations are interpreted restrictively.
245.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

246.text: Article 83 - General conditions for imposing administrative fines: Each supervisory authority must ensure that fines are effective, proportionate and dissuasive. Art. 83(4) - lower tier: fines of up to EUR 10 million, or in the case of an undertaking up to 2 percent of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, for infringements of the obligations of the controller and processor under Articles 8, 11, 25 to 39 and 42 and 43 (including data protection by design, processor contracts, security and breach notification). Art. 83(5) - higher tier: fines of up to EUR 20 million, or up to 4 percent of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for infringements of the basic principles for processing including conditions for consent (Articles 5, 6, 7 and 9), data subjects' rights (Articles 12 to 22), transfers to third countries (Articles 44 to 49), and non-compliance with an order of a supervisory authority. In deciding the amount, authorities consider the nature, gravity and duration, whether the infringement was intentional or negligent, mitigating actions, degree of responsibility, previous infringements, cooperation, categories of data affected (such as health data), and how the infringement became known.
246.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

247.text: EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 on consent: Valid consent under the GDPR must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, given by a statement or clear affirmative action. Freely given: there must be real choice and control; consent is not freely given if there is a clear imbalance of power, such as between a public authority or employer and an individual, or if consent is bundled as a condition for a service. Specific: consent must be tied to a defined purpose; granularity is needed where there are several purposes. Informed: the data subject must know at least the controller's identity, each purpose, the types of data, the right to withdraw, use for automated decisions and transfer risks. Unambiguous: pre-ticked boxes and silence or inactivity are not consent. Explicit consent, required for special category data under Art. 9(2)(a), needs an express statement of consent, for example a written statement or a two-stage verification. The Guidelines note that in clinical research, consent under the GDPR as a lawful basis is distinct from informed consent to participate in a clinical trial, and that scientific research may rely on broader consent to areas of research when ethical standards are respected.
247.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

248.text: EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification: A personal data breach is a breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data. Breaches are classified as confidentiality, integrity or availability breaches, and a temporary loss of availability, such as a hospital system being unavailable, can itself be a breach. A controller is considered 'aware' when it has a reasonable degree of certainty that a security incident has occurred that has led to personal data being compromised; the 72-hour clock under Art. 33 starts then. The controller assesses risk using the type of breach, nature, sensitivity and volume of data, ease of identification, severity of consequences, special characteristics of the individual, and number of affected individuals. Health data breaches usually pose a high risk because of potential discrimination, identity theft and physical or reputational harm. Where a controller is not established in the EU and has no lead supervisory authority under the one-stop-shop mechanism, it must notify each supervisory authority in the Member States where affected individuals reside. Ransomware that causes loss of availability, with a backup restored promptly, may still require notification depending on risk.
248.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

249.text: EDPB Guidelines 03/2020 on the processing of data concerning health for the purpose of scientific research: Confirms that the GDPR and Art. 89 provide a specific regime for scientific research and that special category health data may be processed for research only if there is both an Art. 6 lawful basis and an Art. 9(2) condition. Relevant Art. 9(2) conditions are explicit consent (a), public interest in public health (i), and scientific research (j) based on Union or Member State law. Researchers must respect the data protection principles of Art. 5, with data minimisation, storage limitation and security, and implement the safeguards of Art. 89(1), such as pseudonymisation and, where research aims can be met, anonymisation. Transparency: data subjects must be informed, with limited exceptions where providing information would prove impossible or involve disproportionate effort. Data subject rights may be restricted for research under Art. 89(2) where national law so provides. International transfers for research follow Ch. V: adequacy, appropriate safeguards or narrowly interpreted derogations.
249.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

250.text: EU Artificial Intelligence Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, entered into force on 1 August 2024. Art. 6 classification of high-risk AI systems: an AI system is high-risk if it is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and subject to third-party conformity assessment; this includes AI used in medical devices under the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and in vitro diagnostic devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/746. AI systems in Annex III areas are also high-risk, including access to essential public services and benefits such as eligibility for public healthcare, emergency healthcare patient triage and dispatch systems, and risk assessment and pricing for health and life insurance. Providers of high-risk systems must establish a risk management system (Art. 9), meet data and data governance quality requirements for training, validation and test sets (Art. 10), keep technical documentation and logs (Articles 11 and 12), ensure transparency and instructions for use (Art. 13), design for effective human oversight (Art. 14), and achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Art. 15). Application dates: prohibited practices from 2 February 2025; general-purpose AI rules from 2 August 2025; most high-risk obligations from 2 August 2026; obligations for high-risk AI in Annex I regulated products from 2 August 2027. Proposals to adjust these timelines have been made, so the current dates should be verified. Fines for the most serious infringements reach EUR 35 million or 7 percent of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99).
250.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

251.text: EU Medical Devices Regulation (MDR), Regulation (EU) 2017/745, Annex VIII Rule 11: Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is classified as class IIa, except if such decisions have an impact that may cause death or an irreversible deterioration of a person's state of health, in which case it is class III, or a serious deterioration of health or a surgical intervention, in which case it is class IIb. Software intended to monitor physiological processes is class IIa, or class IIb if it monitors vital physiological parameters where variations could result in immediate danger to the patient. All other software is class I. Software classified above class I requires conformity assessment by a notified body, a quality management system, clinical evaluation, post-market surveillance, and registration in EUDAMED with a unique device identifier. The MDR applies from 26 May 2021. Medical device software that is also a high-risk AI system is subject to the AI Act requirements alongside the MDR.
251.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

252.text: NIS2 Directive, Directive (EU) 2022/2555, which Member States had to transpose by 17 October 2024: Sets cybersecurity risk management and incident reporting obligations for essential and important entities. The health sector is listed in Annex I (sectors of high criticality) and covers healthcare providers, EU reference laboratories, entities carrying out research and development of medicinal products, manufacturers of basic pharmaceutical products and preparations, and manufacturers of medical devices considered critical during a public health emergency. Art. 21 requires appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organisational measures including risk analysis and information system security policies, incident handling, business continuity such as backup management and disaster recovery, supply chain security, vulnerability handling, cryptography and encryption, access control and multi-factor authentication. Art. 23 incident reporting: an early warning to the CSIRT or competent authority within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident, an incident notification within 72 hours, and a final report within one month. Management bodies must approve and oversee the measures and can be held liable. Fines for essential entities reach at least EUR 10 million or 2 percent of worldwide annual turnover.
252.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

253.text: EU Data Act, Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, applicable from 12 September 2025: Gives users of connected products and related services, including connected medical and wellness devices, the right to access and share the data generated by their use, and obliges data holders to make such data available to the user and to third parties chosen by the user on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms. Personal data in such datasets remain subject to the GDPR, and the Data Act does not create a legal basis for processing it. It also contains rules on switching between data processing (cloud) services and on unfair contractual terms in data sharing. Data Governance Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/868, applicable since 24 September 2023: sets conditions for re-use of protected public-sector data (including health data), regulates data intermediation services, and creates a framework for data altruism organisations that collect data made available voluntarily by individuals or companies for general-interest purposes, such as scientific research. The European Health Data Space builds on both instruments for secondary use of health data.
253.article: Data Act Chapters II-III; DGA Chapter IV
253.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

254.text: UK Data Protection Act 2018 (s. 10 and Schedule 1): s. 10 supplements UK GDPR Art. 9 by setting out the conditions under which special category data, including health data, may be processed under Art. 9(2)(b), (h), (i) and (j). Schedule 1 Part 1 conditions relating to employment, health and research: paragraph 1 employment, social security and social protection; paragraph 2 health or social care purposes, which covers preventive or occupational medicine, medical diagnosis, the provision of health care or treatment, and the management of health care systems, where the data are processed by or under the responsibility of a health professional or social work professional or another person who owes a duty of confidentiality; paragraph 3 public health, where processing is carried out by or under the responsibility of a health professional or another person who owes a duty of confidentiality, in the public interest; and paragraph 4 research, where processing is necessary for archiving, scientific or historical research or statistical purposes, is in the public interest and complies with UK GDPR Art. 89(1). Most Schedule 1 conditions require an appropriate policy document describing safeguards and retention (Part 4).
254.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

255.text: UK Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, which received Royal Assent on 19 June 2025: Amends the UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018 and the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations, with provisions being brought into force in stages by regulations. Key changes for health data: a statutory definition of scientific research that covers research that could reasonably be described as scientific, whether publicly or privately funded, and a broader ability to obtain consent for an area of scientific research; a new lawful basis of recognised legitimate interests for specified purposes without a balancing test; replacement of UK GDPR Art. 22 with new Articles 22A to 22D, which permit more automated decision-making, with safeguards, but restrict solely automated decisions based on special category data to certain conditions; a controller's duty to take reasonable and proportionate steps in response to subject access requests; and a statutory complaints process that requires data subjects to complain to the controller first. It converts the Information Commissioner's Office into a corporate body, the Information Commission, increases PECR fines to UK GDPR levels, and establishes digital verification services and smart data schemes. The Act also provides for common information standards for health and adult social care IT.
255.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

256.text: Section 251 of the NHS Act 2006 and the Health Service (Control of Patient Information) Regulations 2002: Allow confidential patient information to be processed without consent for medical purposes in England and Wales where it is not practicable to obtain consent and anonymised information cannot achieve the purpose, setting aside the common law duty of confidentiality. Medical purposes include medical research and the management of health and social care services. Regulation 2 covers communicable diseases and other risks to public health, regulation 3 covers cancer registries, and regulation 5 covers applications for support for other medical purposes. In England the Confidentiality Advisory Group (CAG) of the Health Research Authority advises on applications for research, and the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care makes decisions on non-research applications. Support is time-limited, reviewed annually, and conditional on safeguards, security, and the National Data Opt-out. s. 251 support is a legal gateway for the common law only; the processing still needs a UK GDPR lawful basis and Art. 9 condition. s. 251 support is not required where processing relies on consent, or where the data are anonymised.
256.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

257.text: UK common law duty of confidentiality in health care: Information given in confidence, including patient information held by clinicians, generally may not be disclosed without the individual's consent, a legal duty such as a court order or statute, or an overriding public interest. Implied consent: for the provision of direct care, the National Data Guardian and the Caldicott Principles accept that patients reasonably expect relevant information to be shared among the health and care professionals who are involved in their care, so explicit consent is not needed, provided the patient has been informed and has not objected. Sharing for purposes beyond direct care, such as research, planning and commissioning, generally needs consent, a s. 251 approval, or the use of anonymised data; the National Data Opt-out applies to most such uses of confidential patient information. Public interest disclosures, for example to prevent serious crime or serious harm, are assessed case by case. The duty of confidentiality continues after death. Caldicott Guardians in each organisation advise on these decisions. Note that the legal basis for processing under the UK GDPR is separate from the common law.
257.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

258.text: NHS Records Management Code of Practice 2021: Sets minimum retention periods for health and care records in England, which apply to paper and electronic records. Adult health records, including GP records: 8 years after the last contact, or, for GP records of a deceased patient, 10 years after death. Children's records: until the child's 25th birthday, or until their 26th birthday if they were 17 at the conclusion of treatment. Mental health records, for patients under the Mental Health Act: 20 years after the last entry, or 8 years after death if the patient died while in care. Maternity records and some obstetric and cancer records: 25 years after the last contact. Records of people who lack capacity or who have a diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease have longer periods. At the end of the retention period, records must be reviewed and then either destroyed securely, with an auditable destruction log, or preserved if of archive value; records should not be kept longer than necessary, in line with UK GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) storage limitation.
258.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

259.text: Clinical safety standards for health IT in England, mandated under s. 250 of the Health and Social Care Act 2012: DCB0129 (Clinical Risk Management: its Application in the Manufacture of Health IT Systems) applies to manufacturers and suppliers of health IT. DCB0160 (Clinical Risk Management: its Application in the Deployment and Use of Health IT Systems) applies to the health and care organisations that deploy and use them. Both require a clinical risk management system and process, a named Clinical Safety Officer (a suitably qualified and experienced clinician), a Clinical Risk Management Plan, a Hazard Log that records hazards, causes, controls, and residual risks, and a Clinical Safety Case Report that argues the system is safe for deployment. Organisations must monitor safety after go-live and keep the hazard log up to date. The standards underpin NHS assurance for digital tools, including the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC), which also covers data protection, technical security, interoperability and usability and accessibility. Software that is a medical device must also comply with the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002 and be UKCA or CE marked.
259.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

260.text: MHRA regulation of software and AI as a medical device in Great Britain: Software is a medical device if the manufacturer intends it for a medical purpose such as diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis, treatment or alleviation of disease. It is regulated under the Medical Devices Regulations 2002 (SI 2002/618), as amended. Manufacturers must determine the device class, apply a UKCA mark (CE marking is currently also accepted for a transition period) through a UK Approved Body for higher classes, register the device with the MHRA, and operate post-market surveillance, including vigilance reporting of serious incidents. The Software and AI as a Medical Device Change Programme sets out work to provide clearer guidance and requirements, including on predetermined change control plans, good machine learning practice (aligned with FDA and Health Canada principles) and transparency, and the MHRA AI Airlock regulatory sandbox for testing AI as a medical device. The programme parallels the EU MDR and AI Act in Europe and FDA oversight in the United States.

261.text: UK Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 (NIS Regulations): Implement the EU NIS Directive in UK law and require operators of essential services, including NHS trusts, health boards and other healthcare providers in the health sector, to take appropriate and proportionate technical and organisational measures to manage risks to the security of network and information systems and to minimise the impact of incidents. Competent authorities for the health sector are the Department of Health and Social Care for England, with the Information Commissioner as the competent authority for relevant digital service providers. Operators must notify their competent authority without undue delay and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of an incident that has a significant impact on the continuity of the essential service. Penalties of up to GBP 17 million apply to the most serious failures. The NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT), which maps to the National Cyber Security Centre's Cyber Assessment Framework, is the means by which NHS organisations show compliance. The UK is considering new cyber security legislation that would update the regulations.
261.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

262.text: ICO guidance on personal data breaches under the UK GDPR: Controllers must report a notifiable personal data breach to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms. If the breach is likely to result in a high risk, such as disclosure of health or medical records, the controller must also tell the affected individuals without undue delay. A report is made through the ICO's online form or helpline. NHS organisations and other health and care providers using the Data Security and Protection Toolkit report incidents through the DSPT incident reporting tool, which sends the report to the ICO, NHS England and the Department of Health and Social Care as appropriate. Controllers must keep a record of all breaches, including those not reported, and be able to show the reasoning. Processors must tell controllers without undue delay. Failure to report a notifiable breach can attract a fixed penalty of up to GBP 8.7 million or 2 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher; the higher maximum of GBP 17.5 million or 4 percent applies to infringements of the principles and data subject rights. This corresponds to HIPAA's 60-day deadline in the US.
262.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

263.text: NHS Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC): A national baseline of five areas against which suppliers of digital health technologies, such as apps and software, must show assurance when selling to the NHS and adult social care. The five sections are: company information; clinical safety (including compliance with DCB0129 and a named Clinical Safety Officer); data protection (including a data protection impact assessment, a data processing role, UK GDPR compliance and the Data Security and Protection Toolkit); technical security (including Cyber Essentials Plus, penetration testing and secure development); and interoperability (including use of standards such as HL7 FHIR, SNOMED CT and NHS Number use). A usability and accessibility section requires a product accessible under WCAG 2.2 AA standards. Medical device software also needs UKCA or CE marking. The DTAC is a standard form completed by suppliers and reviewed by commissioners; it does not replace procurement due diligence.
263.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

264.text: HL7 International Patient Summary (IPS) FHIR Implementation Guide: Defines a minimal, specialty-agnostic, condition-independent dataset of essential health information for unscheduled, cross-border care, expressed as a FHIR Composition inside a Bundle of type document. Required sections include problems, allergies and intolerances, and medications; recommended sections include immunisations, results, procedures, medical devices, and advance directives. Profiles include Patient, Condition, AllergyIntolerance, MedicationStatement and MedicationRequest, Observation, Immunization and Procedure, using terminologies such as SNOMED CT for conditions and procedures, LOINC for observations and results, and ATC or national codes for medicines. The IPS is the basis for the European Patient Summary in MyHealth@EU and for the EHDS priority category 'patient summaries', and is used by UK and US initiatives, including the IPS-based Patient Summary specifications in HL7 Europe. It is mapped to CDA templates for legacy systems.
264.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary

265.text: Clinical terminologies used with FHIR and national health data models: SNOMED CT is a comprehensive multilingual clinical terminology of concepts, descriptions and relationships, used for problems, findings, procedures and clinical documentation; it is mandated in NHS England and is a required terminology in the US for problems and procedures under USCDI. LOINC (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes) identifies laboratory tests and clinical observations such as vital signs, for example LOINC 8867-4 for heart rate and 29463-7 for body weight. ICD-10 is the WHO classification of diseases used for diagnosis coding and statistics; the US uses ICD-10-CM for diagnoses and ICD-10-PCS for inpatient procedures, and the UK uses ICD-10 with the OPCS-4 procedure classification. RxNorm, maintained by the US National Library of Medicine, normalises clinical drug names for US interoperability; the UK equivalent is the NHS Dictionary of Medicines and Devices (dm+d). FHIR resources bind coded elements to these code systems using CodeableConcept, system URIs and value sets, which supports semantic interoperability between UK Core, US Core and the European EHDS exchange format.

266.text: FHIR resources for accountability: The Provenance resource records the entities and processes involved in producing, delivering or influencing a resource, including who (agent), what (entity), when (recorded) and why (reason), and may carry a digital signature. It supports tracing the origin and authorship of clinical data. The AuditEvent resource records security-relevant events, such as a user reading a patient record, a query, a login or a break-glass emergency override, with the type and subtype of the action, outcome, recorded time, the agent (user or system), the source system, and the entities (such as the patient) involved. AuditEvent records satisfy audit-control requirements such as the HIPAA Security Rule 45 CFR 164.312(b), GDPR accountability (Art. 5(2)) and Art. 32 expectations, the NHS DSPT, and the EHDS requirement to log access to electronic health data. Implementations commonly use the IHE ATNA profile with FHIR AuditEvent. Consent decisions can be linked with the Consent resource so that disclosures can be shown to match recorded patient preferences.
266.source_hierarchy: primary law > regulator guidance > official technical standard > secondary commentary
